# Players Returning from Achilles, ACL and Other Major Injuries

<sub>Proposed by the synthesis, not on the user's list.</sub>

**Summary.** Players back from Achilles or ACL tears will usually have their minutes managed, sit back-to-backs and lose some efficiency in their first season back. The market tends to overreact to this. In our 9-cat H2H league, price them at a discount to their healthy value but bid above the room's fear. Your playoffs end on 2027-03-28, and that is when the minutes limits matter least.

## Timelines: count the months before you bid

A full Achilles tear usually takes 9 to 12 months to heal, and closer to 12 is more common. A partial tear can take about 6 months. One expert thinks a full 12 months or more off after an Achilles tear may help a player come back stronger than a 9 to 11 month return. ([10-04](https://youtu.be/tnzmsYUA4yQ?t=1614), [08-10](https://youtu.be/sfCe7fS9daM?t=990))

A normal ACL return takes about 12 months. A player who is more than 12 months past a torn ACL can be expected back at full health. ([08-12](https://youtu.be/yoCTTlJ_tPQ?t=874))

What to do: before the auction on 2026-10-18, write down the injury date for every returning player you might bid on. Count the months to opening night. A full Achilles or ACL tear well past 12 months is close to a normal draft pick. A full Achilles tear near the 9 month mark is still a ramp-up case. If he will miss the opening weeks, one of your 4 IL slots can hold him without costing you a starter. ([10-04](https://youtu.be/tnzmsYUA4yQ?t=1614), [08-12](https://youtu.be/yoCTTlJ_tPQ?t=874))

## What the first season back looks like

Players back from injury usually play under minutes limits and miss back-to-backs, and that lowers their value. This has a hidden cost on top of missed games. While a player ramps back up, all of his numbers drop because he plays fewer minutes. ([10-04](https://youtu.be/tnzmsYUA4yQ?t=1700), [07-20](https://youtu.be/-KS_AZjZnw4?t=386))

Achilles returnees rarely play both games of a back-to-back. Over the last 10 years basically only Wes Matthews did, and he played heavily reduced minutes in the second game. ACL returnees usually have their minutes managed and sit back-to-backs early on. Older players back from major injuries will likely sit back-to-backs early in the season. ([08-10](https://youtu.be/sfCe7fS9daM?t=885), [08-22](https://youtu.be/LXZLrL90crE?t=1128), [07-27](https://youtu.be/0AptxcRW0RE?t=1484))

Efficiency usually drops. After an Achilles injury the loss shows up mostly on two-point shots and finishing. In our league that matters most for players whose value comes from FG% on inside shots, because FG% is a team ratio. Play style matters too. Players who rely on IQ and strength come back from an ACL better than speed-based players like Zach LaVine. ([10-01](https://youtu.be/EGdhmUgPAWY?t=394), [07-16](https://youtu.be/-y6p5PYLf00?t=1251), [08-22](https://youtu.be/LXZLrL90crE?t=1152))

Back-to-backs hurt more on teams that play many of them. Before you bid, check the team's back-to-back count. Expect him to miss most of those second games early in the season. ([09-29](https://youtu.be/XSPJL_mlFXo?t=1930))

## Where the experts disagree

On efficiency and long-term level: one note says players back from major ACL or Achilles injuries almost always lose efficiency in their first season back. Another says recent Achilles returnees have mostly come back close to their old level, and that the old rule of an automatic 10% career drop no longer holds. Both can be true: plan for a weaker first season, but do not price in a permanent decline. ([07-16](https://youtu.be/-y6p5PYLf00?t=1251), [08-10](https://youtu.be/sfCe7fS9daM?t=974))

On new injuries: one expert warns that Achilles returnees risk compensation injuries elsewhere in the body. Another says soreness on the other side after major lower-body surgery is common and does not by itself make a player injury-prone. A third note adds that some players lose production for a long time even after a minor injury, so a truly injury-prone player can hurt you for longer than the injury itself. ([09-24](https://youtu.be/_vbAP5y182A?t=518), [07-30](https://youtu.be/TiiaNZCJNs8?t=1524), [08-22](https://youtu.be/KLogvUwv_d8?t=1747))

On back-to-back schedules: one expert says teams with many back-to-backs hurt returning players more. Others say back-to-back counts matter mostly for injury-prone players, and that most back-to-back problems come from in-season injuries nobody can predict. In practice, check the schedule for known returnees but do not let it decide your draft. ([09-29](https://youtu.be/XSPJL_mlFXo?t=1930), [09-29](https://youtu.be/sf6Ga9k-r-Q?t=1686), [08-16](https://youtu.be/gf_6GveiAls?t=1058))

## How to price them in our auction

The market is too scared. Drafters overreact to players coming back from injuries that cost them last season, and you can be more confident than their ADP suggests. Part of the reason is the outdated belief in a permanent drop, which recent Achilles returnees have mostly disproved. ([09-21](https://youtu.be/egRrai3Ax38?t=1258), [08-10](https://youtu.be/sfCe7fS9daM?t=974))

A simple pricing rule: start from what he would be worth healthy. Take off the second games of back-to-backs he will likely skip early in the season and the lower minutes while he ramps up. If his value depends on FG% from finishing, take off a bit more for the first-season efficiency loss. Bid up to that number. The room will often stop below it, and that gap is your edge. ([10-04](https://youtu.be/tnzmsYUA4yQ?t=1700), [07-20](https://youtu.be/-KS_AZjZnw4?t=386), [10-01](https://youtu.be/EGdhmUgPAWY?t=394), [09-21](https://youtu.be/egRrai3Ax38?t=1258))

Our format helps. In H2H the regular season only needs enough wins to make the playoffs, and the playoffs are weeks 19 to 21, ending 2027-03-28. The notes describe minutes management and skipped back-to-backs as early-season issues. By March a player who is now ramping up should be closer to full use. Prefer returnees who are 12 months or more past the injury, and IQ and strength players over speed players. ([08-22](https://youtu.be/LXZLrL90crE?t=1128), [07-27](https://youtu.be/0AptxcRW0RE?t=1484), [08-10](https://youtu.be/sfCe7fS9daM?t=990), [08-22](https://youtu.be/LXZLrL90crE?t=1152))

Also look at older prospects who missed their rookie year to injury. They tend to get bumped down rankings, so they can come cheap in the last rounds of the 144 picks or sit on waivers. ([08-02](https://youtu.be/TOn-D1SV7a8?t=217))

## Managing them during the season

With daily lineups, a skipped back-to-back only costs you if you leave the slot empty. On those nights, use a bench or Util player, or a waiver streamer. Keep your 6 adds per week in mind when you plan streams around his off nights. ([10-04](https://youtu.be/tnzmsYUA4yQ?t=1700), [08-10](https://youtu.be/sfCe7fS9daM?t=885))

When an older returnee sits a back-to-back, his backup gets more games. If you own the returnee, his backup is a useful cheap pickup on those nights. ([07-27](https://youtu.be/0AptxcRW0RE?t=1484))

For trades, an early ramp-up period with soft numbers is a good time to buy from a nervous manager. Make the deal before the 2027-03-04 deadline, while the minutes limits are still holding his stats down. If a returnee's production stays down long after the ramp-up should be over, treat it as the lingering case the notes warn about and sell or bench him. ([07-20](https://youtu.be/-KS_AZjZnw4?t=386), [09-21](https://youtu.be/egRrai3Ax38?t=1258), [08-22](https://youtu.be/KLogvUwv_d8?t=1747))
